svg.text: Bond breaking and the free radical substitution of alkanes
Homolytic fission (Figure 11.5): one electron to each atom
Cl:Cl --(UV light, hv)--> Cl. + Cl. (free radicals)
a free radical has an unpaired electron and is very reactive,
because unpaired electrons tend to become paired
Heterolytic fission (Figure 11.6): both electrons to one atom
shown by full curly arrows in mechanisms
reaction mechanism: the series of steps that make up the overall reaction
Why alkanes are unreactive to polar reagents (11.4)

g.text: paraffins (Latin parum = little, affinis = affinity): inert to acids, alkalis,
oxidising and reducing agents under ordinary conditions
electronegativity C 2.5 and H 2.1 differ little, so C-H and C-C bonding
electrons are shared almost equally: non-polar bonds
sigma bonds hold their electrons tightly between the nuclei: very stable,
a lot of energy is needed to break them
reactions of alkanes (11.5): thermal and catalytic (combustion, cracking),
and free radical substitution (one atom or group replaced by another)
halogen reactivity: F2 (violent) greater than Cl2 greater than Br2 greater than I2 (too slow)

svg.text: Free radical chlorination of methane (11.5.1): in sunlight or UV light

g.text: 1. Initiation: the Cl-Cl bond breaks homolytically using UV energy
2. Propagation: radicals attack the alkane, making new radicals (a chain)
3. Termination: two radicals combine; the chain stops
CH4 + Cl. --> CH3. + HCl
CH3. + Cl2 --> CH3Cl + Cl. (the new Cl. continues the chain)
Cl. + Cl. --> Cl2
CH3. + Cl. --> CH3Cl
CH3. + CH3. --> CH3CH3 (ethane, in traces)
products by repeated substitution (more Cl2, more chlorine atoms per molecule):
CH4 -> CH3Cl -> CH2Cl2 -> CHCl3 -> CCl4
chloromethane, dichloromethane, trichloromethane (chloroform),
tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride); extent depends on the
amount of halogen used; haloalkanes are anaesthetic and toxic

svg.text: the trace of ethane (two methyl radicals joining) is evidence for the free radical mechanism
iodine does not substitute directly (too slow and reversible); fluorine gives carbon, fluoroalkanes and HF violently
